size.note: Shoulder height 66–100 cm follows Wikipedia. Boars can reach 150 kg, although 60–80 kg is described as more common; sows are given as 45–70 kg. The male range entered here is 60–150 kg, with the more common 60–80 kg recorded in this note. Head-and-body and tail lengths were not found as published ranges.

summary: A thick-coated wild pig of dense cover, with pointed, tasselled ears and a contrasting face mask. Southern animals are dark reddish, sometimes almost black, with a paler mane. It is mainly nocturnal, and it runs with the tail held down. It occurs in Kruger but is not often seen in daylight.
description: Adults stand 66–100 cm at the shoulder. The coat in southern populations is dark reddish, sometimes almost black, and it darkens with age. A paler, often whitish dorsal mane or crest may bristle when the animal is agitated. The head has a contrasting face mask of dark and pale markings, or may be almost whitish, and the ears are pointed and tasselled with long hair. The tusks are fairly short and inconspicuous compared with a warthog's. Old boars develop two warts on the snout. Piglets are born with pale yellowish longitudinal stripes on a dark brown background; the stripes soon fade and the coat becomes reddish brown, with a black-and-white dorsal crest.
habits: Bushpigs are mainly nocturnal and lie up in dense thickets by day. They move in sounders with overlapping home ranges, and they are not strictly territorial. They snort and grunt while foraging or when alarmed. Unlike warthogs, they run with the tail held down, and they do not hide in aardvark burrows. In Kruger they are seldom seen from a vehicle in daylight.

diet.summary: An omnivore. In South Africa about 40% of the diet has been recorded as tubers and other underground plant parts, 30% herbage, 13% fruit and some animal matter. They also take roots, succulent plants, insects, rotten wood and, on occasion, small animals.
items: tubers and other underground plant parts

young: One to nine young are born, usually three, after a gestation of eight to ten months. Piglets have pale yellowish stripes on a dark brown coat, which soon fade. They are kept in a nest of plant debris for about four months while they wean. Exact farrowing months for Kruger were not found.
habitat: Forests, woodland, riverine vegetation and other dense cover. In Kruger it is present but hard to see, and the few research-grade records are from thickly wooded areas such as Makuleke.

similar.note: The warthog has a sparsely haired body, large curved tusks and facial warts, and it runs with the tail held up in open country. The bushpig has a full coat, tasselled ears and a face mask, short tusks, and it runs with the tail held down.

population.notes: No recent Kruger population figure was found. The EWT assessment gives regional status as Least Concern and the regional trend as stable, but it does not give a Kruger count. A more accurate figure may be available at this URL: https://www.sanparks.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/KNP-wildlife-trends.pdf.

viewNotes.note: A heavy, thick-coated animal with tasselled ears, a pale face and a bristling dorsal crest. The live photographs used here were taken outside Kruger.
The reddish-brown coat and paler mane are clear from the side. The tail is held down, not up.

calls.description: They snort and grunt harshly while foraging or when alarmed.
